plan.title: How Docker Works
plan.summary: You will understand how Docker packages an app with everything it needs into an image, and runs that image as an isolated container that shares the computer's operating system kernel.

prerequisites.explanation: The core part of an operating system (like Linux) that controls the hardware: memory, CPU, files and network. Every program asks the kernel when it needs these things.
A program that is currently running. One computer can run many processes at the same time, and the kernel keeps track of all of them.
The extra pieces an app needs to run, such as libraries (reusable code), a language runtime like Python, and configuration files.
Software that imitates a whole computer, including its own full operating system and kernel, running on top of a real computer.

analogy.text: Think of a shipping container. Goods are packed once into a standard box, and any ship, train or truck can carry it without caring what is inside. Docker packs an app and its dependencies into a standard 'box' that any machine with Docker can run. The analogy breaks down in one way: Docker containers are not sealed and independent like steel boxes. They all share the host computer's kernel, so the isolation is weaker than it sounds.

plan.visualGuide: A large 'Host Computer' rectangle often fills the lower part of the canvas, with a 'Linux Kernel' bar along its bottom in muted colour. Containers appear as rounded boxes sitting on top of the kernel bar, each holding an 'App' box and a small stack of library blocks. Images are drawn as vertical stacks of flat layer blocks on the left, and the Registry is a cloud-like box at the top right. Active shows what is happening now, new marks things being created (built layers, new containers, writable layers), accent marks data or commands moving along arrows, danger marks conflicts or limits being hit, and muted is background context.

steps.title: The 'works on my machine' problem
steps.caption: An app runs fine on a developer's laptop but fails on a server. Usually the server has different versions of dependencies, such as an older Python or a missing library.

visual.description: Two computer boxes side by side: 'Laptop' on the left and 'Server' on the right. Each contains an 'App' box resting on a stack of dependency blocks. Laptop's stack reads 'Python 3.12' and 'libssl 3'. An arrow labelled 'copy app' moves the App box from Laptop to Server. Server's stack reads 'Python 3.8' with no 'libssl 3'. The App on the server turns danger colour with a small 'error' label.
visual.whatChanges: The copied app turns red because the server's dependencies differ.

steps.title: Package app with dependencies
steps.caption: Docker's idea: ship the app together with everything it needs, not just the app. This package is called an image. It holds the files, libraries and settings, but no kernel.

visual.description: In the center, the App box and its dependency blocks ('Python 3.12', 'libssl 3', 'config') slide together and a rounded outline closes around them, labelled 'Image'. A small note under the outline says 'no kernel inside'. The outline appears in the new colour.
visual.whatChanges: The app and its dependencies get wrapped together into one Image.

steps.title: Dockerfile: the recipe
steps.caption: An image is built from a Dockerfile, a text file of instructions. Each instruction, like 'start from Python' or 'copy my code', describes one step of building the image.

visual.description: On the left, a code panel titled 'Dockerfile' shows four lines: 'FROM python:3.12', 'COPY requirements.txt .', 'RUN pip install -r requirements.txt', 'COPY . .'. An arrow labelled 'docker build' points right to an empty area where the Image will appear. Each line highlights in turn in the active colour.
visual.whatChanges: Each Dockerfile line highlights one after another as the build runs.

steps.title: Images are stacked layers
steps.caption: Steps that add or change files each create a read-only layer, a saved set of file changes. Stacked together, the layers form the image's full file system. Unchanged layers are cached and reused, so rebuilds are fast.

visual.description: The Dockerfile panel stays on the left. On the right, a vertical stack builds from the bottom up, one block per line: 'python:3.12 base', 'requirements.txt', 'installed packages', 'your code'. Each block appears in the new colour as its line is highlighted. Then the code changes and the build runs again: the bottom three blocks get a 'cached' tag in muted colour, and only the top 'your code' block is rebuilt in the new colour.
visual.whatChanges: Layers stack up one per step, and on a rebuild only the changed top layer is remade.

steps.title: Running an image: a container
steps.caption: A container is a running instance of an image. Docker adds a thin writable layer on top of the read-only image layers. Any files the app creates or changes go into that top layer only.

visual.description: The layer stack from the previous step sits on the left. An arrow labelled 'docker run' points right to a copy of the same stack inside a rounded 'Container' outline. A new thin block in the new colour appears on top, labelled 'writable layer'. A small accent dot labelled 'new file' drops into the writable layer, while the layers below stay unchanged.
visual.whatChanges: A writable layer is added on top of the image to make a running container.

steps.title: Many containers, one image
steps.caption: You can start several containers from the same image. They share its read-only layers, and each gets its own writable layer. Deleting a container deletes its writable layer.

visual.description: One image layer stack sits in the center bottom. Three Container outlines above it, labelled 'Container A', 'B' and 'C', each have their own thin writable layer, with dashed lines down to the shared image stack. Then Container C turns danger colour and fades away, taking its writable layer with it, while the image stays.
visual.whatChanges: Three containers share one image, then one is removed along with its writable layer.

steps.title: Containers share the kernel
steps.caption: A container is not a virtual machine. It is a normal process on the host, using the host's own Linux kernel. That is why containers start in about a second and use little memory.

visual.description: Split canvas. Left side titled 'Virtual Machines': a Host box with a 'Hypervisor' bar, and two VM boxes each containing 'App', 'Libraries' and their own 'Guest Kernel' block. Right side titled 'Containers': a Host box with one 'Linux Kernel' bar at the bottom and three small Container boxes containing 'App' and 'Libraries', all resting directly on the kernel bar. The single shared kernel bar on the right highlights in the active colour.
visual.whatChanges: The single shared kernel under all containers highlights, in contrast to each VM's own kernel.

steps.title: Namespaces give each container its own view
steps.caption: Linux namespaces are a kernel feature that limits what a process can see. Each container gets its own file system, process list, network and hostname, so it seems to be alone on the machine.

visual.description: The Host box with the Linux Kernel bar at the bottom. Two Container boxes sit on it. Inside each container appear small labelled panels: 'files', 'processes', 'network', 'hostname'. An eye icon in Container A looks sideways at Container B, and a dashed wall between them turns active colour, blocking the view. Container A's process list shows only its own processes, numbered from 'PID 1'.
visual.whatChanges: A wall appears between containers, so each sees only its own files, processes and network.

steps.title: Cgroups limit resources
steps.caption: Control groups (cgroups) are another kernel feature. They cap how much CPU and memory each container may use, so one greedy container cannot starve the others.

visual.description: Same Host layout. Each container has two gauges beside it: 'CPU' and 'Memory', with a limit line marked on each, e.g. 'max 512 MB'. Container A's memory gauge fills up and stops at its limit line, which turns danger colour, while Container B's gauges stay steady.
visual.whatChanges: Container A's memory rises to its cgroup limit and is stopped there.

steps.title: Client, daemon and registry
steps.caption: You type commands into the Docker client. It sends them to the Docker daemon, a background program that builds images and runs containers. Images are shared through a registry, such as Docker Hub.

visual.description: Left: a code panel 'Docker client' showing 'docker run nginx'. Center: a box 'Docker daemon' inside the Host. Top right: a cloud box 'Registry (Docker Hub)' holding image stacks. An accent message arrow goes client → daemon labelled 'run nginx'. The daemon checks its local image store, finds nothing, then an arrow goes daemon → registry labelled 'pull'. An image stack travels back down to the daemon. Finally a new Container box appears on the Host.
visual.whatChanges: A command travels from client to daemon, the image is pulled from the registry, and a container starts.

steps.title: Docker on Windows and Mac
steps.caption: Linux containers need a Linux kernel. On Windows and macOS, Docker Desktop quietly runs a small Linux virtual machine, and the containers run inside it.

visual.description: An outer box labelled 'Windows or macOS'. Inside it, a box labelled 'Lightweight Linux VM' fades in using the new colour, containing a 'Linux Kernel' bar with two Container boxes on top. The 'Docker client' panel sits outside the VM on the left with an accent arrow into the VM's 'Docker daemon'.
visual.whatChanges: A hidden Linux VM appears around the containers on a non-Linux computer.

plan.recap: Docker packages an app with all its dependencies into an image, built from a Dockerfile as a stack of read-only layers. Running an image creates a container by adding a thin writable layer on top. Containers are ordinary processes that share the host's Linux kernel, kept apart by namespaces and limited by cgroups. The Docker client sends commands to the daemon, which pulls images from registries and runs containers. On Windows and macOS, a small Linux VM provides the kernel those containers need.
